verses.1: Al-Mizan reads huwa as ḍamīr al-shaʾn or ḍamīr al-qiṣṣah: a pronoun without an antecedent that highlights the importance of the following statement. Allah is the Arabic proper name of God. Aḥad, derived from waḥdah, differs from wāḥid: wāḥid can be one among an actual or imaginable plurality and can therefore become many, whereas any supposed second to what is aḥad collapses into the first and adds nothing. Accordingly, “No one (aḥad) came” excludes one, two, and more, while “Not one (wāḥid) came” need not exclude two or more. Aḥad is consequently normally used in negations and is affirmatively predicated only of God. Al-Mizan cites a sermon attributed to Imam ʿAlī: everything described by waḥdah is little except God.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan derives al-ṣamad from seeking, or seeking with reliance. Although exegetes give several formulations, they converge on the chief or master to whom people resort for needs; stated without qualification, it means the One sought for every need. Because God gives all other shayʾ existence, every such thing depends wholly on Him in essence, existence, properties, and traits. “All creation and command belong to Him” (7:54) and the unqualified al-muntahá in (53:42) show Him as the ultimate end of every search, the One who brings it to fruition and fulfills every need.

The definite article in al-ṣamad therefore marks God alone as the absolute object of resort, whereas aḥad needs no article because its affirmative meaning belongs to God alone. Repeating Allah rather than using a pronoun, or joining the two clauses, makes each statement independently sufficient to introduce God; together they describe His essence through uniqueness and His acts through being the terminus to which all return. Al-Mizan also records the reading of ṣamad as muṣmat, “full, solid, not hollow,” which denotes that God neither eats, drinks, sleeps, is born, nor begets; on that reading, (112:3) interprets al-ṣamad.
verses.3: Al-Mizan treats the verses as three unrestricted negations: God neither produces anything by division from His kind, nor derives from another, nor has any peer in essence or acts—creating beings and governing their affairs. Although no one posits multiple Necessary Beings, people assign independent domains of action to lesser lords; any supposedly self-sufficient being, force, or act thereby becomes an equal, whereas every contingent depends on God. Though the negations can derive from aḥadiyyah, they follow more immediately from ṣamadiyyah: begetting implies divisibility, composition, and need for parts; being begotten implies dependence on a parent; equality requires independence within the shared domain. Together with God’s being ṣamad, they establish His absolute oneness in essence, attributes, and acts, while all others’ essence, attributes, and actions emanate from Him. Restricting “equal” to a spouse is therefore unwarranted, because the verse denies every counterpart whatsoever.
